entries.1:1: This book begins by saying that the message came from God to the prophet Habakkuk, who then passed it on. It reminds the reader that what follows is God's word, not just one man's opinion.
entries.1:2: Habakkuk cries out to God, asking how long it will be before God listens, since he keeps praying about violence but nothing seems to change. It shows that honest complaining to God is allowed, and that waiting on him can feel painfully long.
entries.1:3: The prophet says he is forced to watch wrongdoing, destruction, fighting, and arguing all around him. It reflects the grief of seeing evil everywhere and feeling helpless to stop it.
entries.1:4: Because of the evil, the law has no effect and justice never gets done, while wicked people surround those who are in the right. It describes what happens when a society stops enforcing what is fair.
entries.1:5: God answers by telling the people to look at the nations and be amazed, because he is about to do something so surprising they would not believe it even if told. It means God is not idle, and his response may be far beyond what we expect.
entries.1:6: God says he is raising up the Babylonians, a harsh and fast-moving nation that marches across the earth to seize land that is not theirs. It shows that God can use even a ruthless power to carry out his purposes.
entries.1:7: This nation is terrifying, and it makes its own rules about what is right instead of following any higher standard. It warns about the danger of people who answer to no one but themselves.
entries.1:8: Their horses are faster than leopards and their riders are fiercer than wolves at dusk, swooping down like an eagle on its prey. The picture is of an army that strikes suddenly and shows no mercy.
entries.1:9: They all come bent on violence, moving straight ahead, and they take so many captives they are like sand on the seashore. It shows how overwhelming and unstoppable this invasion will feel.
entries.1:10: This enemy mocks kings and laughs at rulers, and no fortified city can stop them because they simply build ramps and capture it. It means human power and defenses are no match for them.
entries.1:11: Then they sweep past like the wind and are gone, but they are guilty because they treat their own strength as their god. It warns that success can lead people to worship their own power instead of God.
entries.1:12: Habakkuk responds by affirming that God is eternal and holy and that his people will not be destroyed, and he recognizes that God has appointed this enemy to discipline them. It holds together trust in God's character with the hard truth that he allows correction.
entries.1:13: The prophet says God is too pure to look at evil and cannot tolerate wrong, so he asks why God seems to watch quietly while wicked people swallow up those better than themselves. It voices the deep question of why God allows injustice to go on.
entries.1:14: He complains that God has made people like fish in the sea or crawling things with no leader to protect them. It expresses the feeling of being helpless and unprotected in the face of a stronger power.
entries.1:15: The enemy catches people like a fisherman hooking fish and gathering them in nets, and he celebrates his catch. It pictures how easily and joyfully the powerful destroy the weak.
entries.1:16: Because his nets bring him such wealth and plenty, the enemy offers sacrifices and burns incense to them. It shows how people end up worshiping the very means by which they gain power and success.
entries.1:17: The prophet asks whether this enemy will keep on emptying his net and destroying nations without ever stopping. It is a plea for God to set a limit on cruelty and bring it to an end.
entries.2:1: The prophet says he will stand watch like a guard on a tower and wait to hear what God answers his complaint. It means we can bring our hard questions to God and then wait quietly for his response.
entries.2:2: God tells him to write the vision down clearly so anyone reading it can understand and pass it on. It means God's message is meant to be clear and shared, not kept hidden.
entries.2:3: The promised vision will come at the right time, and even if it seems slow, it will surely happen. It means we should keep trusting and waiting, because God keeps his promises.
entries.2:4: The proud person is not pleasing to God, but the honest person lives by trusting God. It means real life comes from faith and integrity, not from arrogance.
entries.2:5: The proud, greedy person is never satisfied and grabs everything like death itself. It means greed destroys a person and makes them want more and more.
entries.2:6: The people he has cheated will mock him and pronounce woe on the one who piles up what isn't his. It means those who exploit others will eventually be called out and shamed.
entries.2:7: His victims will suddenly turn on him and make him their prey. It means the harm you do to others can come back on you when they rise up.
entries.2:8: Because he plundered many nations, the rest will plunder him in return for the blood he shed. It means violence and theft bring their own punishment.
entries.2:9: Woe to the one who gains wealth by crooked means to secure his family and keep himself safe. It means building your security on wrongdoing never truly protects you.
entries.2:10: His schemes have brought shame on his own household and harm to his own soul. It means sin against others also damages you and the people closest to you.
entries.2:11: The very stones and wood of his house will cry out against him. It means wrongdoing cannot stay hidden; even the walls will testify against it.
entries.2:12: Woe to the one who builds a city with bloodshed and injustice. It means anything built on cruelty and wrong is under God's judgment.
entries.2:13: God himself sees that people's hard labor for such evil ends up as fuel for fire and comes to nothing. It means God will not let unjust labor last.
entries.2:14: The whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory, like water covering the sea. It means God's greatness will one day be known everywhere.
entries.2:15: Woe to the one who makes his neighbor drunk to expose him to shame. It means using others for your own amusement or advantage is condemned.
entries.2:16: He will be filled with shame instead of glory, and the cup of judgment will come to him. It means the proud will be humbled and receive what they deserve.
entries.2:17: The violence done to Lebanon and its animals will fall back on him for the bloodshed and harm he caused. It means cruelty to land, creatures, and people will not go unpunished.
entries.2:18: An idol made by a person is useless, and trusting in a speechless false god gains nothing. It means things we make into gods cannot help us.
entries.2:19: Woe to the one who tells wood or stone to wake up and teach, when there is no breath in it. It means lifeless idols are powerless, and calling on them is foolish.
entries.2:20: The Lord is in his holy temple, so the whole earth should be silent before him. It means God is real and present, and he deserves our reverent attention.
entries.3:1: This verse is a title noting that what follows is a prayer by the prophet Habakkuk, set to a particular tune. It reminds the reader that this song was meant to be prayed and sung, not just read.
entries.3:2: Habakkuk has heard about God's great deeds and asks God to repeat them in his own day, while asking for mercy even when God is angry. Readers can honestly ask God to act again and to show mercy in hard times.
entries.3:3: God is pictured coming from the regions south of Israel, with his glory filling the sky and the earth echoing his praise. The point is that God's arrival is overwhelming and impossible to miss.
entries.3:4: God's coming is described as radiant light, with power streaming from him yet partly hidden. It means God's strength is real and glorious, even when we cannot see all of it.
entries.3:5: Plague and fire are pictured going ahead of God like servants clearing his path. This shows that God's presence is powerful and even dangerous to anything that opposes him.
entries.3:6: When God stands up, the earth shakes and even ancient mountains crumble, showing that his ways last forever. Readers can trust that God's purposes outlast every human power.
entries.3:7: The tents of nearby peoples tremble in fear at God's approach. It shows that no nation or camp is secure when God comes in judgment.
entries.3:8: The prophet asks whether God's anger is aimed at rivers and sea, picturing him riding out to rescue his people. It means God's power over nature is in service of saving those who belong to him.
entries.3:9: God's bow is drawn and ready, and rivers split open before him. The image shows that God is fully prepared to act and that nothing in nature can stop him.
entries.3:10: Mountains, clouds, and the deep all react with fear, and even the sun and moon stop still. All creation recognizes God's authority when he acts.
entries.3:11: The sun and moon are pictured fleeing from the flash of God's arrows and spear. It means God's weapons, whatever form they take, are more powerful than anything in the sky or on earth.
entries.3:12: God is described marching through the land and crushing nations in his anger. This is a sober picture of God's judgment on those who oppose him and harm others.
entries.3:13: God goes out to rescue his people and his chosen king, striking down the leader of the wicked. Readers can be confident that God fights for those who belong to him.
entries.3:14: The enemy's own weapons are turned against him, and those who delighted in secretly hurting the poor are defeated. It shows that God sees cruelty done in secret and will answer it.
entries.3:15: God's horses walk over the sea and through deep waters, showing his mastery over chaos and danger. Nothing too deep or threatening can keep God from his people.
entries.3:16: Habakkuk is so shaken by the vision that his body trembles and his legs give way, yet he waits quietly for the day of trouble. It is honest to feel afraid of hard times while still trusting God.
entries.3:17: The prophet lists total disaster: no figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, or cattle. Everything a person depends on for food and income could fail at once.
entries.3:18: Even if all those crops and animals are gone, Habakkuk says he will still rejoice in the Lord. His joy rests in God himself, not in good circumstances, and that is where the reader's hope can rest too.
entries.3:19: God gives strength to stand on high places. He makes the climb possible, not painless.
